cells.tense: You're at the table while this grows — deciding what it needs next, saying so out loud, letting the result carry your name.
cells.ask: Announce one thing you're growing: say what it is and how long you've been at it. That puts the work in your name where anyone can see it, and the care stays exactly as it was — you just give it a record.
cells.core:
You're growing something and you're not pretending otherwise. You know what it needs, you know how long it's been going, and you don't hand it off to be finished by someone else. What you've kept alive stays yours because you kept living in it.

The harder part is naming that without a full ledger first. You can keep the work and still let it be known — one honest sentence about what it is and how long you've carried it. Saying so doesn't change what you're doing, and most people find the day stays the same with both things now on record.
cells.sheetLine: You're growing what's in front of you, and you own it.
cells.verb: to tend what grows, with one eye on what it's becoming
cells.place: in the part of life that's trying to be fully, honestly itself

cells.tense: You're living ahead of the growing — squinting at a version you can't see yet, feeding it twice as hard so it arrives already handled.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're growing and leave the next step unwritten: let it get one day older under its own weight. It gives the shape back to what's actually here, and returns your hold to the size of the thing in front of you.
cells.core:
You're running the care ahead of the thing being cared for — deciding what it will need before it has told you, padding the future so it lands soft. That's care turned up too high: it has to keep proving itself against what hasn't happened yet. The work is real; the extra weight is your body getting ready for a scene that hasn't been written.

Growth that isn't forced looks like watering a plant exactly as it asks — pulled back when the soil's still wet, given when it's dry. The next day you leave alone tells you something a plan can't: what the thing does on its own, and that you were still holding the trowel. Both are useful.

cells.tense: You're standing back from the growing — something at the starting block got left there, and the daily work isn't happening now.
cells.ask: Put one hour into the loudest unfinished thing you've got: fix it, water it, or get it into a stranger-proof state. Done-ness is what growing feeds on, and one hour tells you whether this is still yours to keep or something to hand off.
cells.core:
The effort to keep it going has gone quiet — not because it lost its shine, but because you stopped bringing it anything. What you're calling patience is the same thing as standing in the doorway while the room stays empty. A plant can't tell the difference between being left alone and being abandoned.

Past the season when this went well, you had a rhythm: what got done, got un-done, got done again, and the whole thing grew without much drama. Spend an hour making the thing a little more finished, and the strength to keep going tends to come back with it — not for big decisions, just for the next small repair. What's left when you look at the watered plant is usually information, not verdict.

cells.tense: You're already growing what you are — picking what to feed it, what to leave behind — and you're not calling that the steering; it reads as just how the days go.
cells.ask: Put the truth of one cared-for thing on a postcard to the person who should know: this kept going because you kept it alive. Doing it tells whoever receives it that the effort counted, and leaves you holding the handle to what you've been driving all along.
cells.core:
The steering is happening — you choose what the days are made of, what gets saved and what gets left — but somewhere you stopped signing the choices. It's all still yours, and the story about it has a smaller part for you than the moves you're making. The growing is real; the hand that keeps it so is offstage.

Credited, it's simple — you say what you're growing and why it's still alive, and the name on the work is yours. One postcard does the whole move in public: the plant, the hands, the years it took. The work stays exactly the same; the receipt says whose it is.
cells.sheetLine: The growing is happening. The record just doesn't have your name on it yet.

attempts.check: The unsupported claims that could creep in are biographical: that tending was once punished, or that the person is hiding something they made. The record says nothing about what happened, only that the capacity sits unbalanced in this seat; the cells keep the locating to what the capacity does, not what the life did. A reader might reasonably say 'I'm not holding back growing on purpose — I just don't know what could come of what I've tended,' and the ask still works for them, because it only asks for one plain announcement, no story required. The sentence that risked serving the writer over the reader is any line about the person believing someone else made their growth — it would sound like an accusation; the cells instead describe how the capacity is currently credited, not what the person believes.
